note: The neutral all-purpose greeting, also used for goodbye ('Hei hei'). Borrowed from Swedish 'hej'. 'Moi' and 'Terve' are the informal alternatives.
Literally the adjective 'healthy'; the same root gives 'terveys' (health) and 'Tervetuloa' (welcome). Common between friends and in shops.
Wishes take the partitive case: 'hyvä huomen' becomes 'hyvää huomenta'. 'Huomenta!' alone is a common shortening.
From 'ilta' (evening) in the partitive. Used from late afternoon onwards; 'Iltaa!' is the short form.
From 'yö' (night), partitive 'yötä'. Said only when someone is going to bed, not as an evening goodbye. Note the vowel harmony: front vowels y and ö take '-tä'.
Doubling the greeting turns it into a goodbye: 'Moi' = hi, 'Moi moi' = bye. Very common in Helsinki speech; 'Moikka' is another playful variant.
The doubled 'Hei' means goodbye, just like 'Moi moi'. Neutral enough for shops and offices.
Passive present of 'nähdä' (to see). The passive doubles as a casual 'let's': 'Nähdään huomenna' = see you tomorrow. 'Moi, nähdään!' is a standard sign-off.
The standard 'how are you'. The usual answer is 'Kiitos, hyvää' or 'Ei mitään erikoista' (nothing special). Spoken Finnish also uses 'Miten menee?' (how's it going?).
The set reply to 'Mitä kuuluu?'. 'Hyvää' is the partitive of 'hyvä', matching the partitive in the question.
'Paljon' means 'a lot'. 'Kiitoksia' (plural) is a slightly warmer 'many thanks'; 'Kiitti' is slangy.
The everyday reply to thanks; 'kestää' means to last or to bear, so the sense is 'no trouble'. 'Ole hyvä' is the other reply and also means 'here you are'.

example.en: – Thanks for the help! – You're welcome.

note: A compound of 'terve' (healthy) and 'tulo' (coming), a calque of Swedish 'välkommen'. Also used on signs and when greeting guests at the door.
'Hauska' means fun or pleasant and 'tutustua' means to get to know. A near-synonym is 'Hauska tavata' (nice to meet).
The formal 'yes'. In speech 'Joo' is far more common, and Finns often answer by repeating the verb: 'Tuletko?' – 'Tulen.' (Are you coming? – I come.)
'Ei' is also the negative verb and conjugates for person: en, et, ei, emme, ette, eivät. 'En tiedä' = I don't know. On its own 'Ei' is the plain 'no'.
The spoken-language yes, borrowed from Swedish 'jo'. Expect to hear 'joo joo' and 'juu' as well. Use 'Kyllä' in formal writing.
Standard Finnish marks possession twice: the pronoun 'minun' plus the suffix '-ni' on 'nimi'. In speech this becomes 'Mun nimi on...' or simply 'Olen...' (I am...).
Spoken form: 'Mikä sun nimi on?' ('sinun' shortens to 'sun'). The possessive suffix '-si' means 'your'.
Negation uses the negative verb 'en' plus the bare stem 'ymmärrä' (from 'ymmärtää'). The double 'rr' is the weak grade of 'rt'.
Yes/no questions add '-ko/-kö' to the verb: 'puhut' + 'ko'. Language names are not capitalised in Finnish and take the partitive after 'puhua'.
'Ruokahalu' is a compound of 'ruoka' (food) and 'halu' (desire); as a wish it stands in the partitive. Said by the host or the waiter when the food arrives.
Partitive of 'onni' (luck, happiness). Covers both 'congratulations' and 'good luck': 'Paljon onnea!' at a birthday, 'Onnea kokeeseen!' before an exam.
'Viikonloppu' is a compound: 'viikon' (of the week) + 'loppu' (end). The Friday farewell in every Finnish office.
From the same root as 'terve'. 'Terveisiä Helsingistä!' = greetings from Helsinki; 'Sano terveisiä!' = say hi (to someone) from me.
From Swedish 'noll'. Finnish writes decimals with a comma and reads it 'pilkku': 0,5 = 'nolla pilkku viisi'.
Stem changes: genitive 'yhden', partitive 'yhtä'. In fast speech it shortens to 'yks'. Estonian 'üks' is the cognate.
Genitive 'kahden', partitive 'kahta'. Nouns after any number take the partitive singular: 'kaksi kissaa' (two cats). Spoken: 'kaks'.
Old Uralic word: Estonian 'kolm', Hungarian 'három'. Genitive 'kolmen'.
Estonian 'neli', Hungarian 'négy'. Genitive 'neljän'. Note the vowel harmony: front vowel 'ä' throughout.
Genitive 'viiden', partitive 'viittä'. Estonian 'viis', Hungarian 'öt'. Spoken 'viis'.
Two words look alike: the number 'kuusi' (genitive 'kuuden') and 'kuusi' meaning spruce tree (genitive 'kuusen'). Only the inflected forms tell them apart.
Estonian 'seitse', Hungarian 'hét'. Genitive 'seitsemän' is identical to the basic form. Spoken: 'seittemän'.
Built on 'kah-' (two): historically 'two missing' from ten, matched by 'yhdeksän' (one missing). Estonian 'kaheksa'.
Built on 'yh-' (one) in the same way as 'kahdeksan'. Front vowels, so the ending is '-än'. Estonian 'üheksa'.
Genitive 'kymmenen', partitive 'kymmentä', which appears in all the tens: 'kaksikymmentä' (20). Estonian 'kümme'.
Teens are 'digit + toista', the partitive of 'toinen' (second): one of the second ten. Only the first part inflects: 'yhdentoista'.
Same pattern as 'yksitoista'. 'Kello kaksitoista' = twelve o'clock.
'Viisi' + 'toista'. Likewise kolmetoista 13, neljätoista 14, kuusitoista 16, seitsemäntoista 17, kahdeksantoista 18, yhdeksäntoista 19.
'Kaksi' + 'kymmentä' (partitive of ten). Units follow directly: 'kaksikymmentäyksi' (21). Spoken: 'kakskyt'.
Tens are regular: neljäkymmentä 40, viisikymmentä 50, kuusikymmentä 60, seitsemänkymmentä 70, kahdeksankymmentä 80, yhdeksänkymmentä 90.
An ancient Indo-Iranian loan (compare Sanskrit 'śatam'). Estonian 'sada', Hungarian 'száz'. Gradation: 'sadan'. 'Kaksisataa' = 200.
Genitive 'tuhannen', partitive 'tuhatta'. 'Kaksituhatta' = 2000. Estonian 'tuhat'. Thousands are separated by a space in writing: 10 000.
From Swedish 'miljon'. A noun in Finnish: 'kaksi miljoonaa' (two millions, partitive).
From 'ensi' (first, next): 'ensi viikolla' = next week. Ordinals agree in case like adjectives: 'ensimmäisessä kerroksessa' (on the first floor).
Means both 'second' and 'other, another': 'toinen kerta' (second time), 'toinen kuppi' (another cup). Genitive 'toisen'.
Ordinals from three onward end in '-s': kolmas 3rd, neljäs 4th, viides 5th, kuudes 6th, kymmenes 10th. Genitive 'kolmannen'.
Also means 'side'. Watch the clock: 'puoli kolme' (half three) means 2:30, half-way to three. Genitive 'puolen'. Estonian 'pool'.

example.en: Let's meet at half past five.

note: From Swedish 'par'. 'Pari päivää' = a couple of days; 'pariskunta' = a (married) couple. Takes the partitive like a number.
From Swedish 'nummer'. 'Puhelinnumero' = phone number. 'Luku' is the word for a number as a mathematical quantity or a chapter.
Genitive 'perheen'. 'Perheenjäsen' = family member. The wider clan of relatives is 'suku'.
An old Germanic loan (compare Gothic 'aiþei' = mother). Gradation: 'äidin'. Children say 'äiti' or 'äiskä'.
Native Uralic word: Estonian 'isa'. Combined with 'iso' (big) it gives 'isoisä' (grandfather). Children say 'isi' or 'iskä'.
The plural comparative of 'vanha' (old): parents are 'the older ones'. Singular 'vanhempi' means one parent or simply 'older'.
Genitive 'lapsen', partitive 'lasta', plural 'lapset'. 'Lapsenlapsi' (child's child) = grandchild. Estonian 'laps'.
Means both boy and son. Gradation changes k to j: 'pojan', 'pojat'. 'Poikaystävä' = boyfriend. Estonian 'poeg' (son).
Means both girl and daughter; the formal word for daughter is 'tytär'. Gradation 'tytön'. 'Tyttöystävä' = girlfriend.
Genitive 'veljen', plural 'veljet'. 'Isoveli' = big brother, 'pikkuveli' = little brother.
The everyday word; 'sisar' is the formal variant, an old Baltic loan related to Lithuanian 'sesuo'. 'Isosisko' = big sister.
Compound of 'iso' (big) + 'äiti'. The affectionate words are 'mummo', 'mummi' and 'mummu'.
Compound of 'iso' (big) + 'isä'. Affectionate: 'vaari', 'ukki', 'pappa'.
The warm, everyday word for grandmother, heard far more than 'isoäiti'. Also used for an old lady in general. Variants: 'mummi', 'mummu'.
Genitive 'vaimon'. The husband is 'mies' or 'aviomies' ('avio-' = marital). 'Vaimoni' = my wife.
Means both 'man' and 'husband'. Irregular stem: genitive 'miehen', partitive 'miestä', plural 'miehet'. Estonian 'mees'.
Genitive 'naisen', plural 'naiset'. Related to 'naida' (to marry) and 'naimisissa' (married). Estonian 'naine'.
Gives 'ystävällinen' (friendly) and 'ystävänpäivä' (Valentine's Day, literally friend's day, celebrated for friends in Finland). 'Paras ystävä' = best friend.

example.en: He / she is my best friend.

note: Very common colloquial word for a friend or pal of any gender; also used for 'guy' ('se kaveri' = that guy). 'Työkaveri' = workmate.
A Germanic loan related to English 'neighbour' and Swedish 'nabo'. 'Naapurimaa' = neighbouring country.
A nursery word built on baby-talk sounds. Genitive 'vauvan'. 'Vauvantalo' is a slang name for a maternity hospital.
Derived from 'aika' (time, age). Genitive 'aikuisen'. 'Aikuisten lippu' = adult ticket.
Genitive 'ihmisen', plural 'ihmiset' (people). 'Hän' refers to a person of either gender; 'se' (it) is used for people in casual speech.
Finnish separates the two uncles: 'setä' is the father's brother and 'eno' the mother's brother. 'Setä' is also what children call any unfamiliar man.
Used for aunts on both sides. Like 'setä', children also use it for any grown-up woman: 'tuo täti' = that lady.
Gradation: 'serkun'. 'Pikkuserkku' (little cousin) = second cousin.
From 'näytellä' (to act, to perform). The feminine 'näyttelijätär' with the '-tar/-tär' suffix is now dated; 'näyttelijä' is used for everyone.
Gradation drops the k: 'ruoan' (written) / 'ruuan' (spoken). 'Ruokakauppa' = grocery shop, 'ruokalista' = menu.
An old Germanic loan, related to English 'loaf'. Gradation 'leivän'. Dark 'ruisleipä' is the national staple.
Compound of 'ruis' (rye, genitive 'rukiin') + 'leipä'. Voted Finland's national food in 2017; dense, sour and often sold as flat rings.
The same three letters are also the exclamation 'voi!' (oh!): 'Voi ei!' = oh no! Estonian 'või', Hungarian 'vaj'.
A Germanic loan, related to Swedish 'ost'. 'Leipäjuusto' (bread cheese) is a squeaky baked cheese eaten with cloudberry jam.
Gradation 'maidon'. Finns drink more milk per person than almost anyone; 'piimä' is sour milk, 'rasvaton' = fat-free.
Genitive 'veden', partitive 'vettä'. A core Uralic word: Estonian 'vesi', Hungarian 'víz'. Tap water in Finland is safe and free in restaurants.

example.en: Could I have a glass of water?

note: From Swedish 'kaffe'. Finland has the world's highest coffee consumption per person; 'kahvitauko' (coffee break) is written into labour agreements.
Partitive 'teetä': 'Haluaisin teetä' = I would like (some) tea. Pronounced with a long 'ee', not like English 'tea'.
A Germanic loan related to English 'ale'. Genitive 'oluen', partitive 'olutta'. Slang: 'kalja', 'bisse'.
From Swedish 'vin'. 'Punaviini' = red wine, 'valkoviini' = white wine. Wine above 5.5% is sold only in state 'Alko' shops.
'Lihapullat' = meatballs, 'naudanliha' = beef, 'sianliha' = pork, 'poronliha' = reindeer meat. Estonian 'liha'.
A textbook Uralic cognate: Estonian 'kala', Hungarian 'hal'. 'Lohi' = salmon, 'silakka' = Baltic herring, 'kalakeitto' = fish soup.
Means both the bird and the meat. An old Germanic loan related to German 'Hahn'. 'Broileri' is the usual word for chicken meat in shops.
Estonian 'muna'. 'Kananmuna' (hen's egg) is the full form; 'munakas' = omelette. Also vulgar slang for a testicle, so context matters.
From Swedish 'päron' (pear), via 'jordpäron' (earth pear). 'Uudet perunat' (new potatoes) with dill are a midsummer ritual.
From Swedish 'ris'. 'Riisipuuro' (rice porridge) is the traditional Christmas Eve breakfast, with one almond hidden inside.
From Swedish 'sallad'. Also means lettuce. Loanwords ending in a consonant get a final '-i' in Finnish: salaatti, pankki, bussi.
Also used figuratively, 'työn hedelmä' = fruit of one's labour. Plural 'hedelmät'.
'Omenamehu' = apple juice, 'omenapiirakka' = apple pie. Plural 'omenat', partitive 'omenaa'.
Berries are central to Finnish food: 'mustikka' (bilberry), 'puolukka' (lingonberry), 'lakka' (cloudberry). Everyone may pick them in any forest ('jokamiehenoikeus').

example.en: We pick berries in the forest.

note: From Swedish 'socker'. 'Sokeriton' = sugar-free; the '-ton/-tön' suffix means 'without'.
Estonian 'sool'. 'Suolainen' = salty; 'salmiakki' is the salty liquorice Finns love.
The Finnish breakfast staple, usually kaurapuuro (oat porridge) eaten with milk or jam. Riisipuuro is the Christmas porridge. Genitive puuron.
'Appelsiinimehu' = orange juice. Also 'sap' or 'cordial'; 'mehukatti' is a famous squash brand.
From 'ravinto' (nourishment) + the place suffix '-la', the same suffix as in 'kahvila' and 'sairaala'.
'Kahvi' + '-la'. Cafés are where Finns drink their famous quantity of coffee, usually with a 'pulla' (cardamom bun).

example.en: Shall we go to a café?

note: From 'tarjoilla' (to serve). Used for all genders; the old feminine 'tarjoilijatar' is rarely heard now.
'Ruoka' + 'lista'. The loanword 'menu' is also used, especially for a set menu.
From 'laskea' (to count, to lower): a bill, an invoice, also a downhill slope ('mäenlasku'). Splitting the bill is normal in Finland.
'Kiitos' does the work of 'please' in Finnish. More fully: 'Saisinko laskun?' (Could I have the bill?). Tipping is not expected.
Gradation 'pöydän'. A Germanic loan. 'Pöytävaraus' = table reservation; 'pöydällä' = on the table.

example.en: Do you have a free table?

note: From Swedish 'stol'. Old Finnish could not start a word with two consonants, so loans lost the first one: stol → tuoli, strand → ranta, glas → lasi.
From 'lauta' (board, plank) with the diminutive '-nen'. Genitive 'lautasen'.
From 'haara' (branch, fork of a tree or road). Gradation 'haarukan'.
Genitive 'veitsen', partitive 'veistä'. Related to 'veistää' (to carve). The traditional Finnish belt knife is a 'puukko'.
An old Slavic loan, compare Russian 'ložka'. Gradation 'lusikan'. 'Teelusikka' = teaspoon.
From Swedish 'glas' with the initial g dropped. Means both the material and a drinking glass: 'lasi vettä' = a glass of water.
From Swedish 'kopp'. Gradation 'kupin'. 'Kuppi kahvia' = a cup of coffee.

example.en: I'll have a cup of coffee.

note: 'Vesipullo' = water bottle. Bottles and cans carry a deposit ('pantti') returned at supermarket machines.
From 'aamu' (morning). 'Aamupala' (morning bite) is the everyday synonym. Genitive 'aamiaisen'.
The same word means 'south-west' on a compass. Lunch in Finland is early (11-12) and 'lounasbuffet' deals are everywhere. Genitive 'lounaan'.
From 'päivä' (day): historically the main meal of the day, now the evening meal, often eaten around 5-6 pm.
From 'ilta' (evening); a more formal or later dinner than 'päivällinen'. 'Iltapala' = evening snack.
Compound of 'jälki' (trace, after) + 'ruoka'. 'Alkuruoka' (beginning-food) = starter, 'pääruoka' (head-food) = main course.
From 'herkku' (treat, delicacy). Partitive 'herkullista'. 'Tosi hyvää!' is the everyday way to praise food.
Conditional of 'saada' (to get) plus the question suffix '-ko': the politest way to order. Followed by the partitive: 'Saisinko kahvia?'
Conditional of 'haluta' (to want); the '-isi-' marker makes it polite. 'Haluan' (I want) sounds blunt in a restaurant.
Said while clinking glasses and looking the other person in the eye. Among friends you may also hear 'Skål' (Swedish) or 'Hölkyn kölkyn'.
Finnish has no verb 'to have': 'teillä on' = at you there is. 'Teillä' is the plural/polite 'you'; to a friend say 'Onko sinulla...?'
Also means 'distance': 'pitkä matka' = a long way. 'Matkalla' = on the way; 'Hyvää matkaa!' = have a good trip. Estonian 'matk' means a hike.
Derived from 'matka'. 'Matkustaja' = passenger, 'matkailu' = tourism. 'Matkustan junalla' = I travel by train (adessive case for 'by').

example.en: We travel to Lapland in winter.

note: The same word means 'flag': 'Suomen lippu' = the Finnish flag. Gradation 'lipun'. 'Lipunmyynti' = ticket sales.
From Swedish 'pass'. Gradation 'passin'. 'Henkilökortti' = ID card.
International loan with the usual added '-i'. 'Hotellihuone' = hotel room. Pronounce the double 'll' long.
Genitive 'huoneen'. 'Huoneisto' = apartment, 'makuuhuone' = bedroom, 'kylpyhuone' = bathroom.

example.en: Do you have any rooms available?

note: From 'varata' (to reserve). 'Minulla on varaus' = I have a booking. Genitive 'varauksen'.
From Swedish 'karta'. Gradation 'kartan'. 'Kartalla' = on the map.
Allative case of 'oikea', which also means 'correct, real'. 'Oikealla' (adessive) = on the right. 'Käänny oikealle' = turn right.
From 'vasen' (left). 'Vasemmalla' = on the left. Finnish uses the same case endings for directions as for places: -lle (onto), -lla (at).
'Suoraan' from 'suora' (straight); 'eteenpäin' = 'to the front' + the direction particle '-päin'. 'Mene suoraan' is enough in speech.
Takes the partitive: 'lähellä asemaa' = near the station. 'Lähin' = the nearest; 'lähikauppa' = corner shop.

example.en: The hotel is near the station.

note: 'Kauas' = (to) far away, 'kaukaa' = from far. 'Kaukana' is static: 'Onko se kaukana?' = Is it far?
'Missä' is the inessive of 'mikä'. The answer uses a location case: 'Se on tuolla' (it is over there), 'asemalla' (at the station).
Three-way system: 'täällä' (here), 'siellä' (there, mentioned), 'tuolla' (over there, pointed at). 'Tänne' = to here, 'täältä' = from here.
Used when pointing at something visible. 'Tuonne' = to over there. Compare 'siellä' for a place already mentioned.
From 'pohja' (bottom, base): in the old world-picture the north was the 'bottom' of the sky. 'Pohjois-Suomi' = northern Finland, 'Pohjola' = the mythical North.
From the stem 'ete-' (front): the south was 'the front', facing the midday sun. 'Etelä-Suomi' = southern Finland.
Gradation 'idän'. 'Itä-Suomi' = eastern Finland; 'Itämeri' (East Sea) = the Baltic Sea.
Genitive 'lännen', partitive 'länttä'. 'Länsi-Suomi' = western Finland. Compass points are written with a hyphen before a place name.
Compound of 'lento' (flight) + 'kenttä' (field). The official term is 'lentoasema' (flight station), but everyone says 'lentokenttä'.

example.en: I go to the airport by bus.

note: Also means 'position, status'. 'Rautatieasema' (iron-road station) = railway station, 'linja-autoasema' = bus station. 'Asemalla' = at the station.
'Päästä' means to reach or get somewhere; the destination takes a 'to' case: 'Kuinka pääsen asemalle?' / 'keskustaan?'. 'Miten' is a common synonym for 'kuinka'.

example.en: How do I get to the city centre?

note: 'Lomalla' = on holiday, 'kesäloma' = summer holiday. A public holiday is a 'juhlapyhä', not a 'loma'.

example.en: I am on holiday next week.

note: 'Matka' + 'laukku' (bag). Gradation 'matkalaukun'. 'Käsimatkatavarat' = hand luggage.
Same loan as English 'auto'. 'Autolla' = by car. 'Vuokra-auto' = rental car.
From Swedish 'buss'. The formal word is 'linja-auto' (line car), seen on signs like 'linja-autoasema'.
A 19th-century coinage when railways arrived. 'Junalla' = by train; 'VR' is the state railway company.
'Vaunu' is from Swedish 'vagn'. Helsinki speech says 'ratikka' or the slang 'spora' (from Swedish 'spårvagn').
Helsinki's metro, opened in 1982, is the northernmost in the world. 'Metrolla' = by metro.
'Lento' (flight) + 'kone' (machine). Finnish prefers native compounds for modern inventions: 'tietokone' (computer) is built the same way.
Estonian 'laev'. The Helsinki–Tallinn and Helsinki–Stockholm ferries are 'laivat'; 'laivamatka' = cruise.
'Polkea' = to pedal, 'pyörä' = wheel. In speech just 'pyörä' or the slang 'fillari'. 'Pyörällä' = by bike.

example.en: I ride to work by bike.

note: Spelled with 'ks', as Finnish has no 'x'. 'Taksitolppa' = taxi rank.
From 'pysähtyä' (to come to a stop). Gradation 'pysäkin'. 'Bussipysäkki', 'ratikkapysäkki'.
Used for driving a car, riding a bike and, oddly, shaving: 'ajaa parta' = to shave a beard. 'Ajokortti' = driving licence.
Related to 'käydä' (to go, to visit). 'Kävely' = a walk, 'kävelykatu' = pedestrian street.

example.en: I walk to work every day.

note: Consonant gradation 'nt' → 'nn' in the weak forms: 'lennän'. 'Lento' = flight, 'lentolippu' = plane ticket.
Estonian 'tee'. The verb 'tietää' (to know) is derived from it: to know is to know the way. 'Moottoritie' = motorway.
From Swedish 'gata' (Finnish turned the g into k). Gradation 'kadun'. 'Kadulla' = on the street. Many Helsinki streets are signed in both Finnish and Swedish.
An old Baltic loan (compare Lithuanian 'tiltas'). Gradation 'sillan'. 'Sillalla' = on the bridge.
From Swedish 'bensin'. In speech 'bensa'; 'bensa-asema' or 'huoltoasema' = petrol station.
From 'liikkua' (to move). 'Liikennevalot' = traffic lights, 'julkinen liikenne' = public transport. Genitive 'liikenteen'.
'Aika' + 'taulu' (board, from Swedish 'tavla'). Also 'schedule' in general: 'aikataulussa' = on schedule.
'Olen myöhässä' = I'm late; 'juna on myöhässä' = the train is late. For 'late at night' use 'myöhään'.
Gradation 'lautan'. The boat to Suomenlinna fortress is a 'lautta'; big car ferries are usually called 'laiva'.
Estonian 'sadam'. 'Satamassa' = in the harbour. Helsinki has the Länsisatama (West Harbour) and Eteläsatama (South Harbour).
'Ajo' (driving, from 'ajaa') + 'kortti' (card, from Swedish 'kort'). Gradation 'ajokortin'.
'Parkki' is colloquial for parking; the official word is 'pysäköintipaikka'. 'Paikka' = place. Gradation 'parkkipaikan'.
Means to rise, get up and board: 'nousta bussiin' (illative) = get on the bus. Getting off is 'jäädä pois' or 'nousta pois'.

example.en: I get on the train in Tampere.

note: Gradation 'ajan'. As an adverb it means 'quite': 'aika hyvä' = quite good. 'Ajoissa' = on time.
Estonian 'päev'. 'Päivää!' is a greeting, 'tänä päivänä' = today, 'joka päivä' = every day.
A Germanic loan, compare Swedish 'vecka'. Gradation 'viikon'. 'Ensi viikolla' = next week, 'viime viikolla' = last week.
'Kuu' (moon, also 'month' on its own) + 'kausi' (period, season). All month names end in '-kuu'.
Genitive 'vuoden', partitive 'vuotta'. 'Hyvää uutta vuotta!' = Happy New Year. 'Olen 30-vuotias' = I am 30 years old.
An old Germanic loan (Swedish 'stund') that lost its initial 's'. Also a school lesson: 'suomen tunti' = Finnish class. Gradation 'tunnin'.
From Swedish 'minut'. Gradation 'minuutin'. 'Viisi minuuttia' = five minutes (partitive after the number).
A contraction of 'tänä päivänä' (on this day). 'Tänä iltana' = this evening, 'tänä vuonna' = this year.
The essive of 'huomen' (morning), the same word as in 'Hyvää huomenta'. 'Ylihuomenna' = the day after tomorrow.
'Toissapäivänä' = the day before yesterday. 'Eilinen' = yesterday's: 'eilinen lehti' = yesterday's paper.
Estonian 'nüüd'. 'Nyt heti' = right now; 'nykyään' = nowadays.
'Kello' means clock, watch and bell. Answer: 'Kello on kolme' (it is three). 'Mitä kello on?' is the other common wording.

example.target: – Paljonko kello on? – Kello on puoli neljä.
example.en: – What time is it? – It's half past three.

note: Borrowed from Old Swedish 'mānadagher' (moon day); the '-tai' ending of all weekday names comes from Scandinavian 'dag'. Days are written in lower case.

example.en: On Monday I go to work.

note: From Swedish 'tisdag', the day of the Norse god Tyr. 'Tiistaina' = on Tuesday (essive case for 'on a day').
The one native weekday name: 'keski' (middle) + 'viikko' (week), like German 'Mittwoch'. Gradation 'keskiviikon', 'keskiviikkona' = on Wednesday.
From Swedish 'torsdag', Thor's day. 'Torstaina' = on Thursday.
From Old Swedish 'fredagher', named after the goddess Frigg; the f became p because old Finnish had no f. 'Perjantaina' = on Friday.
From Old Norse 'laugardagr', 'washing day', via Swedish 'lördag'. Fittingly, Saturday is still the traditional sauna evening in Finland.

example.en: On Saturday we heat the sauna.

note: From Swedish 'söndag'. 'Sunnuntaina' = on Sunday. Shops in Finland now open on Sundays too.
All twelve months are native compounds ending in '-kuu' (moon). 'Tammi' means oak, but here it is usually explained as 'core, axis', the heart of winter. Months are lower-case.
'Kesä' = summer. Midsummer ('juhannus') falls in late June and is the biggest summer holiday. 'Kesäkuussa' = in June.
'Joulu' (Christmas) is a Scandinavian loan, compare Swedish 'jul'. The other months: helmikuu, maaliskuu, huhtikuu, toukokuu, heinäkuu, elokuu, syyskuu, lokakuu, marraskuu.
'Aamulla' = in the morning, 'aamupala' = breakfast, 'aamuisin' = in the mornings. 'Huomen' is the older word kept in 'Hyvää huomenta'.
Gradation 'illan', 'illalla' = in the evening. 'Iltapäivä' (evening-day) = afternoon; 'iltapala' = evening snack.

example.en: What are you doing this evening?

note: Genitive 'viikon' + 'loppu' (end). 'Viikonloppuna' = at the weekend. Gradation 'viikonlopun'.
From Swedish 'färg', with the f turned into v. 'Värikäs' = colourful, 'värittää' = to colour in.
From 'puna' (redness). Colour adjectives in '-inen' have genitive '-isen': 'punaisen'. 'Punaviini' = red wine.
An old Slavic loan, compare Russian 'siniy'. The flag is the 'siniristilippu' (blue-cross flag). Genitive 'sinisen'.
Partitive 'vihreää'. 'Vihreät' = the Greens (party); 'vihannes' = vegetable comes from the same root.
From 'kelta', an old Baltic loan (compare Lithuanian 'geltas'). 'Keltainen' is also the colour of the Finnish post.
Estonian 'must'. 'Mustikka' (bilberry) is literally 'the black one'. 'Musta kahvi' = black coffee.
Related to 'valo' (light) and 'valkea' (white, also 'fire' in older usage). 'Valkoviini' = white wine. Genitive 'valkoisen'.
Partitive 'harmaata'. 'Harmaa arki' (grey everyday life) is a common phrase; 'harmaa talous' = the black economy.
Same root as 'ruska', the blaze of autumn colours in Lapland that draws hikers every September.
The colour only; the fruit is 'appelsiini' (from Swedish 'apelsin', 'apple from China'). Genitive 'oranssin'.
International loan with the added '-i'. 'Liila' (lilac) is the everyday word for lighter purple.
'Vaalean' (genitive of 'vaalea', light) + 'punainen'. Many shades are built this way: 'tummansininen' = dark blue, 'vaaleanvihreä' = light green. Slang: 'pinkki'.
Used for colours, hair and beer: 'tumma olut'. For darkness as lack of light use 'pimeä'.
'Vaaleat hiukset' = blond hair. Partitive 'vaaleaa'. The opposite is 'tumma'.
Gradation 'muodon'. 'Muotoilu' = design, 'muoti' (fashion) is a different word.
From 'ympäri' (around). 'Liikenneympyrä' = roundabout.
From 'neljä' (four). Also short for square metre: 'asunnossa on 50 neliötä' = the flat has 50 square metres. A town square is 'tori'.
From 'kolme' (three). 'Kolmiodraama' = love triangle.
'Viivakoodi' = barcode. A queue or a route is 'linja', a line of text is 'rivi'.
From 'pyörä' (wheel). 'Pyöreät luvut' = round numbers.
'Suora lähetys' = live broadcast, 'suoraan' = straight, directly. Finns value 'suora puhe', straight talk.
'Jalkapallo' (foot ball) = football, 'pesäpallo' = Finnish baseball, the national sport. 'Maapallo' = the globe.
Estonian 'täht'. Gradation 'tähden'. 'Tähtitiede' = astronomy, 'pohjantähti' = the North Star.
Gradation 'raidan'. 'Raidallinen' = striped; 'raitapaita' = striped shirt.
'Väri' + the adjective suffix '-käs' (full of). Genitive 'värikkään'. Also 'colourful' of a person or story.
Estonian 'pea', Hungarian 'fej'. Also 'end' or 'main': 'pääkaupunki' (head city) = capital, 'päänsärky' = headache.
A core Uralic word: Estonian 'silm', Hungarian 'szem'. 'Silmälasit' (eye glasses) = spectacles.
Estonian 'kõrv'. 'Korvakoru' = earring, 'korvatulppa' = earplug.
Estonian 'nina'. 'Nenäliina' (nose cloth) = handkerchief or tissue.
Estonian 'suu', Hungarian 'száj'. Also the mouth of a river: 'joensuu', hence the city Joensuu.
Genitive 'hampaan', plural 'hampaat'. 'Hammaslääkäri' = dentist, 'hammasharja' = toothbrush.
One word covers hand and arm. Genitive 'käden', partitive 'kättä'. Estonian 'käsi', Hungarian 'kéz'. 'Käsin' = by hand.
One word covers foot and leg. Gradation 'jalan', 'jalat'. 'Jalan' also means 'on foot'; 'jalkapallo' = football. Estonian 'jalg'.
Genitive 'sydämen'. Estonian 'süda', Hungarian 'szív'. 'Sydämellinen' = hearty, warm.
'Maha' is the colloquial word for belly. 'Vatsakipu' = stomach ache; 'vatsa on kipeä' = my stomach hurts.
Gradation 'selän'. Also an open stretch of sea: 'Selkämeri' is the Bothnian Sea. 'Selkäkipu' = back pain.
Genitive 'veren', partitive 'verta'. Estonian 'veri', Hungarian 'vér'. 'Verenpaine' = blood pressure.
From 'terve' (healthy). Genitive 'terveyden'. 'Terveyskeskus' = health centre, the local public clinic. 'Terveydeksi!' = bless you (after a sneeze).
Genitive 'sairaan'. 'Olen sairaana' = I'm ill (essive for a temporary state). 'Sairasloma' = sick leave.
From Swedish 'läkare'. 'Lääkärissä' = at the doctor's. 'Hammaslääkäri' = dentist, 'eläinlääkäri' = vet.
'Sairas' (sick) + the place suffix '-la'. 'Sairaalassa' = in hospital.
From Swedish 'apotek'. Gradation 'apteekin'. Painkillers like 'särkylääke' are sold only in pharmacies.
Genitive 'lääkkeen'. Same root as 'lääkäri'. 'Särkylääke' = painkiller, 'lääkkeet' = medication.
Gradation 'kivun'. 'Kipeä' = sore, hurting: 'kurkku on kipeä' = my throat is sore.
Related to 'kuuma' (hot). 'Minulla on kuumetta' = I have a fever (partitive). 'Kuumemittari' = thermometer.
Shortened from 'influenssa'. Covers the common cold as well: 'olla flunssassa' = to have a cold. Initial 'fl' shows it is a recent loan.
'Sattua' means both 'to hurt' and 'to happen'. The sufferer is in the partitive; add the place: 'Minua sattuu päähän' (my head hurts). 'Sattuuko?' = does it hurt?
Plural of 'hius' (a single hair); hair on the head is always plural. 'Tukka' is the colloquial singular word. 'Hiustenleikkuu' = haircut.
Genitive 'sormen'. 'Sormus' (ring) is derived from it. 'Peukalo' = thumb.
From the same root as 'parempi' (better) and 'paras' (best). 'Parantaa' = to heal or improve (transitive). 'Pikaista paranemista!' = get well soon.
Irregular location forms: 'kotona' (at home), 'kotiin' (home, to home), 'kotoa' (from home). Estonian 'kodu'. 'Kotimaa' = homeland.

example.en: I'm at home in the evening.

note: Estonian 'talu' means a farm. 'Omakotitalo' (own-home house) = detached house, 'kerrostalo' = block of flats, 'rivitalo' = terraced house.
From 'asua' (to live, reside). Gradation 'asunnon'. 'Yksiö' = studio, 'kaksio' = one-bedroom flat (from 'yksi', 'kaksi' rooms).
From 'keittää' (to boil, to cook). 'Keittiössä' = in the kitchen. 'Keitto' = soup.
'Makuu' (lying down, from 'maata' = to lie) + 'huone'. 'Makuupussi' (lying bag) = sleeping bag.
'Kylpy' (bath) + 'huone'. Finnish flats usually have a shower rather than a bathtub, and often a small sauna next to the bathroom.
From the letters 'WC' said the Finnish way (vee-see). The everyday word; signs say 'WC'. 'Vessapaperi' = toilet paper.
'Olo' (being, state) from 'olla' + 'huone'. 'Olohuoneessa' = in the living room.
The one Finnish word every language knows. Finland has roughly three million saunas for 5.5 million people. 'Kiuas' = the stove, 'löyly' = the steam thrown on it.

example.en: Shall we go to the sauna?

note: Genitive 'oven', 'ovella' = at the door. 'Ulko-ovi' = front door; 'ovikello' = doorbell.
An old Slavic loan, compare Russian 'okno'. 'Ikkunalla' = by the window, 'ikkunapaikka' = window seat.
From Swedish 'säng'. Gradation 'sängyn'. 'Sängyssä' = in bed; 'vuode' is the formal word.
From Swedish 'soffa'. 'Sohvalla' = on the sofa. 'Sohvaperuna' = couch potato.
'Jää' (ice) + 'kaappi' (cupboard, from Swedish 'skåp' with the 's' dropped). 'Pakastin' = freezer. Gradation 'jääkaapin'.

example.en: The milk is in the fridge.

note: 'Tieto' (knowledge, data) + 'kone' (machine). Finnish coins native words for technology: 'tietokone', 'kännykkä', 'sähköposti'. Spoken: 'kone' or 'läppäri' (laptop).
From 'puhella' (to chat) + the instrument suffix '-in'. Genitive 'puhelimen'. A mobile is 'kännykkä' (from 'känny', hand), originally a Nokia trademark.
Spoken: 'telkkari' or 'tv' (said 'teevee'). 'Katsoa televisiota' = to watch TV (partitive).
From Swedish 'lampa'. Gradation 'lampun'. 'Valo' = light.
From 'avata' (to open) + the instrument suffix '-in'. Genitive 'avaimen', plural 'avaimet'.
Also 'layer'. Finland counts the ground floor as the first: 'ensimmäinen kerros' = ground floor. 'Kerrostalo' = block of flats. Genitive 'kerroksen'.
From Swedish 'hiss'. 'Hissillä' = by lift. Gradation 'hissin'.
'Pihalla' = out in the yard, but the idiom 'olla pihalla' means to be clueless. 'Takapiha' = back yard.
'Siivous' = cleaning, 'siivooja' = cleaner. 'Pestä' is to wash. Note the stem change: 'siivota' → 'siivoan'.
Only for residing; 'to be alive' is 'elää'. Place in the inessive or adessive: 'Asun Helsingissä' / 'Tampereella'. 'Asukas' = inhabitant.
Gradation 'mökin'. Finland has around half a million 'kesämökit', usually by a lake with a sauna. 'Mökillä' = at the cottage.

example.en: We are at the cottage all July.

note: Plural of 'vaate' (garment). 'Vaatekaappi' = wardrobe, 'vaatekauppa' = clothes shop. Genitive plural 'vaatteiden'.
Gradation 'paidan'. Also the base for 't-paita', 'villapaita' (sweater) and 'kauluspaita' (collared shirt).
Always plural, as in English; a single pair is 'yhdet housut'. 'Housuissa' = in trousers. 'Shortsit' = shorts.
Gradation 'mekon'. 'Leninki' is the more formal word for a dress; 'kesämekko' = summer dress.
Genitive 'hameen'. 'Minihame' = miniskirt. 'Hameväki' is an old joking word for womenfolk.
Gradation 'takin'. 'Talvitakki' = winter coat, 'sadetakki' = raincoat, 'toppatakki' = padded jacket. Coats go on the 'naulakko' (coat rack) at the door.

example.target: Ota takki mukaan, ulkona on kylmä.
example.en: Take a coat, it's cold outside.

note: Plural of 'kenkä'; gradation 'nk' → 'ng': 'kengän'. Shoes come off at the door in every Finnish home. 'Kenkäkauppa' = shoe shop.
Plural of 'sukka' (gradation 'sukan'). Hand-knitted 'villasukat' (wool socks) are a classic Finnish gift.
From Swedish 'hatt'. Gradation 'hatun'. A brimmed hat; the winter knit cap is a 'pipo'.
The essential Finnish winter garment. The idiom 'pipo kireällä' (beanie pulled tight) means uptight, taking things too seriously.
From Swedish 'handske'. The formal word is 'käsineet' (from 'käsi', hand); mittens are 'lapaset'.
'Kaula' (neck) + 'huivi' (scarf, headscarf). Often just 'huivi' in speech.
From 'pukea' (to dress). Gradation 'puvun'. Means a man's suit, a costume ('kansallispuku' = national costume) and 'uimapuku' = swimsuit.
Clipped from 'farmarihousut' (farmer trousers), the name under which jeans were first sold in Finland. Always plural.
Written with a hyphen and a lower-case t. Gradation 't-paidan'.
'Villa' (wool) + 'paita'. Also 'neule' (a knit) or the loan 'pusero'. 'Huppari' = hoodie.
Plural of 'saapas' (genitive 'saappaan'). 'Kumisaappaat' = rubber boots; Nokia made them before it made phones.
'Alus-' (under, base) + 'vaatteet'. 'Alushousut' = underpants, 'alusasu' = lingerie.
'Uima-' (from 'uida', to swim) + 'puku'. 'Uimahousut' = swimming trunks, 'uimahalli' = swimming pool (hall).
The k vanishes in weak forms: 'puen'. 'Pukea päälle' = to put on; 'pukeutua' = to get dressed. 'Puku' (suit) comes from this verb.
'Riisua kengät' = take off one's shoes, the first thing you do in a Finnish home. 'Riisuutua' = to undress oneself.
Also means 'whole, entire': 'koko päivä' = the whole day. Gradation 'koon'. 'Mitä kokoa?' = what size?

example.en: Do you have this in another size?

note: Gradation 'laukun'. 'Käsilaukku' = handbag, 'matkalaukku' = suitcase, 'reppu' = backpack.
'Turvavyö' (safety belt) = seat belt. The '-vyöhyke' in 'aikavyöhyke' (time zone) is the same root, a belt around the earth.
Causative of 'sopia' (to fit, to suit). 'Sovituskoppi' = fitting room. Also 'to adapt, to reconcile'.
'Töissä' (plural inessive) = at work, 'töihin' = to work, 'töistä' = from work. 'Työtön' = unemployed ('-tön' = without).

example.en: I'm at work from eight to four.

note: Means both the place and the job itself: 'Sain työpaikan' = I got a job. Gradation 'työpaikan'.
From Swedish 'skola' with the initial 's' dropped. 'Koulussa' = at school. 'Peruskoulu' = comprehensive school (ages 7-16).
'Yli' (over, upper) + 'opisto' (institute, from 'oppia' = to learn). 'Helsingin yliopisto' = University of Helsinki.
From 'opiskella'. A school pupil is 'oppilas' or 'koululainen'. 'Opiskelijakortti' = student card.
From 'opettaa' (to teach), itself from 'oppia' (to learn). Finnish teachers all hold master's degrees. Children address them as 'ope'.
From 'koota' / 'kokoontua' (to gather). Genitive 'kokouksen'. 'Kokouksessa' = in a meeting; 'palaveri' is the colloquial loan.
From 'toimi' (function, post) + the collective suffix '-sto' (as in 'kirjasto', library). 'Toimistossa' = at the office.
The root of a whole family: 'kirjain' (letter of the alphabet), 'kirje' (letter, mail), 'kirjoittaa' (to write), 'kirjasto' (library).
Covers any writing stick: 'lyijykynä' (lead pen) = pencil, 'kuulakärkikynä' (ball-tip pen) = ballpoint, 'sulkakynä' = quill.
From Swedish 'papper'. Paper and pulp were long Finland's biggest export; 'paperitehdas' = paper mill.
'Sähkö' (electricity, a 19th-century coinage) + 'posti' (post, from Swedish). In speech 'meili' or 'sähköpostiosoite' for the address.
Irregular stem 'tee-/teke-'. 'Mitä sinä teet?' = What are you doing? / What do you do? 'Tehdas' (factory) comes from it. Spoken: 'mä teen'.

example.en: What do you do for a living?

note: For studying a subject or at a university. Object in the partitive: 'opiskelen suomea'. 'Opiskelu' = studies.
Gradation 'pp' → 'p': 'opin'. 'Opettaa' = to teach, 'oppitunti' = lesson. Proverb: 'Oppia ikä kaikki' (one learns all one's life).
The k disappears in weak forms: 'luen'. Also 'to study for': 'lukea kokeeseen'. 'Lukio' = upper secondary school, 'luku' = number or chapter.

example.en: I read the paper in the morning.

note: From 'kirja'. Gradation 'tt' → 't': 'kirjoitan'. 'Kirjoittaja' = writer, 'kirjailija' = author.
From 'työ'. Rather formal; in speech people say 'olla töissä' (to be at work): 'Olen töissä pankissa' = I work at a bank.
Gradation 'palkan'. 'Palkkapäivä' = payday, 'palkinto' = prize or reward.
Colloquial but universal. The formal words are 'esihenkilö' (supervisor) and 'johtaja' (director).
From Swedish 'kollega'. 'Työkaveri' (work mate) is the everyday alternative.
From Swedish 'ingenjör'. Finland trains a very high share of engineers; 'diplomi-insinööri' = engineer with a master's degree.
Usually plural. 'Tehdä läksyt' = to do one's homework; 'kotitehtävät' (home tasks) is the formal word.
Genitive 'kokeen'. Also 'experiment'. 'Ylioppilaskoe' = matriculation exam; a university exam is a 'tentti'.
Gradation 'ammatin'. 'Ammattikoulu' = vocational school, 'ammattilainen' = professional. 'Mikä sinun ammattisi on?' = What is your profession?
Genitive 'sään'. 'Sääennuste' = weather forecast. 'Millainen sää tänään on?' = What's the weather like today?
'Ilma' covers both air and weather; 'ilmasto' = climate. 'Ilman' means 'without', and 'ilmainen' (free of charge) comes from it.
Gradation 'nk' → 'ng': 'auringon'. 'Aurinko paistaa' = the sun is shining; 'aurinkoinen' = sunny.
Genitive 'sateen'. The verb is 'sataa': 'sataa' = it's raining, 'sataa lunta' = it's snowing. 'Sateenvarjo' (rain shade) = umbrella.
Genitive 'lumen', partitive 'lunta'. Estonian 'lumi'. 'Lumiukko' (snow old-man) = snowman, 'lumisade' = snowfall.
Genitive 'tuulen'. 'Tuulee' = it's windy; 'tuulinen' = windy. Estonian 'tuul'.
Genitive 'pilven'. 'Pilvinen' = cloudy. Estonian 'pilv'. 'Pilvipalvelu' = cloud service.
'Minulla on kylmä' = I'm cold (literally 'at me is cold'). 'Pakkanen' is frost, temperatures below zero. Estonian 'külm'.
'Kuumaa kahvia' = hot coffee. A heatwave is 'helle', the summer days over 25 degrees. 'Kuume' (fever) is related.
Irregular stem: genitive 'lämpimän'. 'Lämpötila' (warmth state) = temperature, 'lämmittää' = to heat.
About three quarters of Finland is forest. 'Metsässä' = in the forest. Estonian 'mets'. 'Metsästää' = to hunt.
Genitive 'järven'. Finland is 'tuhansien järvien maa', the land of a thousand lakes; the real count is about 188,000. Estonian 'järv'.

example.en: The cottage is on the lake shore.

note: Genitive 'meren', partitive 'merta'. 'Itämeri' = the Baltic Sea. Estonian 'meri'.
The k disappears: genitive 'joen'. 'Joensuu' (river mouth) is a city. Estonian 'jõgi'.
Genitive 'saaren'. Finland has well over 100,000 islands; 'saaristo' = archipelago. Estonian 'saar'.
Means both tree and wood as a material. Estonian 'puu', Hungarian 'fa'. 'Puutarha' (tree garden) = garden.
Finland's national tree. Birch twigs bundled into a 'vihta' (or 'vasta' in the east) are used to whisk the skin in the sauna.
From 'elää' (to live). Genitive 'eläimen', plural 'eläimet'. 'Eläintarha' = zoo, 'lemmikkieläin' = pet.
Gradation 'linnun'. Estonian 'lind'. 'Lintukoto' (bird home) is a poetic word for a sheltered, idyllic place.
The national animal. Out of old taboo it has many bynames: 'otso', 'kontio', 'mesikämmen' (honey-paw). Also a beer brand.
'Repo' (an old word for fox) + 'tulet' (fires): in folklore a fox running over the fells swept sparks into the sky with its tail. Always plural.

example.en: We saw the northern lights in Lapland.

note: Genitive 'kevään'. 'Keväällä' = in spring. 'Kevätväsymys' (spring tiredness) is a recognised Finnish complaint.
'Kesällä' = in summer. 'Kesämökki' = summer cottage, 'kesäloma' = summer holiday. Midsummer is 'juhannus'.

example.en: In summer it is light even at night.

note: 'Syksyllä' = in autumn. 'Syyskuu' (September) is built on the same stem. 'Ruska' = the autumn colours.
Genitive 'talven'. 'Talvella' = in winter. Estonian 'talv', Hungarian 'tél'. 'Talvisota' = the Winter War of 1939-40.
Gradation 'pp' → 'p': 'kaupan', 'kaupassa' (in the shop). An old Germanic loan related to English 'cheap'. Also means 'trade, deal'.
Originally 'fur, squirrel pelt', the currency of the old fur trade. 'Rahat' (plural) = money one has: 'Minulla ei ole rahaa' = I have no money.
Gradation 'nt' → 'nn': 'hinnan'. 'Hintalappu' = price tag. 'Halpa hinta' = low price.
Gradation 'halvan'. 'Halvempi' = cheaper, 'halvin' = cheapest. 'Edullinen' is the polite 'affordable'.
Genitive 'kalliin'. Also 'dear, beloved' in old-fashioned usage. 'Liian kallis' = too expensive.
'Maksaa' means both 'to cost' and 'to pay'. 'Mitä se maksaa?' is equally common. Answer: 'Se maksaa viisi euroa.'
One verb for both: 'Maksan kortilla' = I pay by card; 'Se maksaa kympin' = it costs a tenner. 'Maksu' = payment, fee.
'Ostos' = a purchase, 'ostokset' = shopping, 'ostoskeskus' = shopping centre. 'Ostan leipää' (partitive = some bread).
'Myytävänä' = for sale, 'myyjä' = shop assistant, 'myynti' = sales. Third person 'myy' is just the stem.
Finland adopted the euro in 2002, replacing the 'markka'. Partitive after numbers: 'kymmenen euroa'. Prices are rounded to 5 cents; 1- and 2-cent coins are not used.
Means both a euro cent and a centimetre. Gradation 'sentin'. 'Viisikymmentä senttiä' = fifty cents.
From Swedish 'kort'. 'Pankkikortti' = bank card, 'kortilla' = by card. Finland is close to cashless; cards work everywhere.
Built on the stem of 'käsi' (hand): money you hold in your hand. 'Käteisellä' = in cash.

example.en: Are you paying in cash or by card?

note: From Swedish 'kvitto'. Gradation 'kuitin'. 'Haluatko kuitin?' (Do you want the receipt?) is what every cashier asks.
From 'alentaa' (to lower). Genitive 'alennuksen'. 'Ale' is the short word for a sale; 'alennusmyynti' = clearance sale.
From Swedish 'torg'. Every Finnish town has one; Helsinki's 'Kauppatori' is by the harbour. 'Torilla' = at the market.
'Kauppa' + 'keskus' (centre). Genitive 'kauppakeskuksen'. 'Ostoskeskus' is a synonym.
From 'ilman' (without), itself from 'ilma' (air). 'Ilmaiseksi' = for free. 'Vapaa' is 'free' in the sense of not occupied.
From Swedish 'kassa'. 'Kassalla' = at the checkout. 'Itsepalvelukassa' = self-service checkout.
From Swedish 'bank' with the added '-i'. Gradation 'pankin'. 'Pankkikortti' = bank card, 'pankkitili' = bank account.
'Lahjakortti' = gift card, 'joululahja' = Christmas present. 'Lahjakas' = gifted, talented.
From 'asia' (matter, business). Genitive 'asiakkaan'. 'Asiakaspalvelu' = customer service.
From 'tarjota' (to offer). Genitive 'tarjouksen'. 'Tarjouksessa' = on special offer.
'Muovipussi' = plastic bag, which you pay for. Cashiers ask 'Tarvitsetko pussin?' (Do you need a bag?). Gradation 'pussin'.
For ordering goods, food or a taxi. 'Tilaus' = an order or subscription. Stem change: 'tilata' → 'tilaan'.
From 'onni' (luck, happiness) with the '-llinen' suffix. Describes a lasting state; for cheerful in the moment use 'iloinen'. Genitive 'onnellisen'.
From 'suru' (sorrow, grief). 'Surullinen uutinen' = sad news. 'Surra' = to grieve.
From 'ilo' (joy). 'Olen iloinen, että tulit' = I'm glad you came. 'Iloisesti' = cheerfully.
From 'viha', which means both anger and hatred. 'Olla vihainen jollekin' = to be angry at someone (allative). 'Vihata' = to hate.
The past participle of 'väsyä' (to get tired). Genitive 'väsyneen'. Alternative: 'Minua väsyttää' (literally 'it tires me').
From 'nälkä' (hunger). More common than the adjective is the 'have' construction 'Minulla on nälkä' (at me is hunger).
From 'jano' (thirst). As with hunger, Finns usually say 'Minulla on jano' (I have thirst) rather than using the adjective.
The standard Finnish pattern for feelings and possession: the person in the adessive ('-lla') plus 'on'. Spoken: 'Mulla on nälkä'. Likewise 'Minulla on jano / kylmä / kiire'.
From 'rakas' (dear, beloved), which is also what you call your partner: 'rakas' = darling. Genitive 'rakkauden'. 'Rakkaudella' = with love.
Object in the partitive: 'Rakastan sinua'. Finns are famously sparing with the phrase; a running joke says it is said once, at the wedding.
From Swedish 'tycka'. Colloquial but universal; the thing liked goes in the elative ('-sta'): 'Tykkään kahvista'. The formal verb is 'pitää' (pidän kahvista). Also 'to like' on social media.
Object in the partitive: 'Pelkään hämähäkkejä' (I'm afraid of spiders). 'Pelko' = fear, 'pelottava' = scary. Stem change: 'pelätä' → 'pelkään'.
'Itku' = crying, tears. Proverb: 'Itku pitkästä ilosta' (tears come from long joy), said when fun ends in tears.
'Nauru' = laughter. To laugh at someone or something takes the allative: 'nauraa vitsille' (laugh at a joke). 'Hymyillä' = to smile.
'Toivo' = hope (also a man's name). 'Toivottavasti' = hopefully; 'toivottaa' = to wish someone something: 'toivottaa hyvää matkaa'.
'Minulla on ikävä sinua' = I miss you (I have a longing for you). As an adjective it means unpleasant or dull; 'ikävä kyllä' = unfortunately.
Gradation 'pelon'. 'Pelätä' = to fear. 'Pelkuri' = coward.
'Ilolla' = with pleasure, gladly. 'Iloinen' = cheerful, 'ilahduttaa' = to delight. 'Ilo' is also used as a girl's name.
International loan with the Finnish '-i'. 'Stressaantunut' = stressed; 'stressata' = to stress (colloquial verb).
Past participle of 'hermostua' (to get nervous or irritated), from 'hermo' (nerve). 'Jännittynyt' = tense, excited before an event.
Finns like to call themselves 'ujo', though reserved ('hiljainen', quiet) is closer. 'Ujostella' = to be shy, to feel awkward.
The all-purpose spoken word of approval: 'Kiva!' = nice!, 'Oli kivaa' = it was fun (partitive). Use 'mukava' or 'hauska' in formal writing.

example.en: It was nice to see you!

note: Takes the elative: 'ylpeä sinusta' = proud of you. 'Ylpeys' = pride. Partitive 'ylpeää'.
Past participle of 'yllättyä' (to be surprised). 'Yllätys' = a surprise, 'yllättää' = to surprise someone.
From 'rauha' (peace). 'Rauhallista joulua' = peaceful Christmas; 'Rauhoitu!' = calm down. Finns prize a 'rauhallinen' person.
Spoken: 'mä meen'. The passive 'Mennään!' means 'Let's go!'. Destination in a 'to' case: 'menen kauppaan', 'menen torille'.
Also 'to become': 'tulee kylmä' = it's getting cold, 'tulla hulluksi' = to go mad. 'Tuletko mukaan?' = Are you coming along? 'Tulevaisuus' = the future.
Estonian 'sööma', Hungarian 'eszik'. Third person 'syö' is the bare stem. A whole object takes the genitive/accusative ('syön omenan'), a partial one the partitive ('syön leipää').
Estonian 'jooma'. 'Juoma' = a drink. Drinks go in the partitive: 'juon kahvia'. 'Juoppo' = a drunkard.
Gradation 'kk' → 'k': 'nukun'. 'Nuku hyvin!' = sleep well. 'Nukahtaa' = to fall asleep, 'uni' = sleep or a dream.
Intransitive: you wake up yourself. 'Herättää' = to wake someone else; 'herätyskello' (waking clock) = alarm clock.
Languages take the partitive: 'puhun suomea'. 'Puhe' = speech, 'puhelin' = telephone (talking device).
Derived from 'tie' (road). Gradation 't' → 'd': 'tiedän'. 'En tiedä' = I don't know. Knowing a person is 'tuntea'; knowing how is 'osata'.
'Haluan' sounds direct; in shops and restaurants soften it to the conditional 'haluaisin'. 'Halu' = desire.
'Voinko auttaa?' = Can I help? Also 'to feel': 'Miten voit?' = How are you? 'Voi' on its own is the sigh 'oh' and also the word for butter.
Gradation 'tt' → 't': 'otan'. Used for ordering: 'Otan kahvin' = I'll have a coffee. 'Ottaa kuva' = to take a photo.
Gradation 'nt' → 'nn': 'annan'. The receiver takes the allative: 'Anna se minulle' = give it to me. 'Anteeksi' (sorry) is built on this verb.
Irregular like 'tehdä': stem 'näe-/näke-'. 'Nähdään!' (see you) is its passive. 'Näkemiin' (goodbye) is literally 'until seeing'.
Object in the partitive for ongoing watching: 'katson televisiota'. 'Katso!' = look! 'Katse' = a glance, gaze.
From 'kuulla' (to hear); 'kuuluu' in 'Mitä kuuluu?' is the same root. Object in the partitive: 'kuuntelen musiikkia'.

example.en: I listen to music on the bus.

note: From 'sana' (word). 'Sanomalehti' (message leaf) = newspaper. 'Miten sanotaan suomeksi...?' = How do you say ... in Finnish?
Gradation 'tt' → 't': 'odotan'. The thing waited for is in the partitive: 'odotan bussia'. 'Odota!' = wait! Also 'to expect': 'odottaa lasta' = to be expecting a baby.
Gradation 'tt' → 't': 'autan'. The person helped is in the partitive: 'auttaa minua'. 'Apu' = help; 'Apua!' = Help!
Three jobs in one: 'pidän kirjaa' (I hold the book), 'pidän kahvista' (I like coffee, elative), 'minun pitää mennä' (I have to go, genitive subject). Gradation 'pidän'.
'Sain lahjan' = I got a gift; 'Saanko?' = May I? 'Saisinko' (conditional) is the polite way to order. 'Saada aikaan' = to achieve.
Gradation 'ht' → 'hd': 'lähden'. 'Lähdetään!' = let's go! 'Lähtö' = departure, on every airport board.

en: to go (and come back) / to visit
note: A round trip: 'käyn kaupassa' = I pop to the shop. Also 'to attend' ('käydä koulua') and 'to suit' ('Käykö huomenna?' = Does tomorrow work?). 'Käy sisään!' = come in.
Gradation 'rt' → 'rr': 'ymmärrän'. 'Ymmärrätkö?' = Do you understand? 'Ymmärrys' = understanding.
Estonian 'istuma'. 'Istu alas' = sit down. 'Istunto' = a session (of parliament), 'istuin' = a seat.
Causative of 'soida' (to ring, to sound). 'Soitan sinulle' = I'll call you (allative); 'soitan kitaraa' = I play the guitar (partitive). Gradation 'soitan'.

example.en: I'll call you in the evening.

note: Inflects for case: 'mikä' (what is), 'minkä' (which one, genitive), 'mitä' (partitive), 'missä' (where), 'miksi' (why). 'Mikä tämä on?' = What is this?
The partitive of 'mikä', used with most verbs: 'Mitä sinä teet?' On its own, 'Mitä?' is the everyday 'What? / Pardon?'. Spoken: 'Mitä sä teet?'
Irregular stem 'kene-': 'kenen' (whose), 'ketä' (whom, partitive), 'kenelle' (to whom). Plural 'ketkä'.
The inessive of 'mikä'. Finnish asks three 'wheres': 'missä' (where at), 'mihin' / 'minne' (where to), 'mistä' (where from).
'Milloin juna lähtee?' = When does the train leave? In speech 'koska' is also used for 'when', although it formally means 'because'.
Historically the translative case of 'mikä'. 'Miksi ei?' = Why not? Answer with 'koska' (because) or 'siksi, että'.
'Kuinka' is the slightly more formal synonym: 'Miten menee?' / 'Kuinka voit?' both mean 'How are you doing?'. 'Miten niin?' = How so?
Direction only: 'Minne menet?' = Where are you going? 'Mihin' is the interchangeable form. 'Minne vain' = anywhere.
Pairs with the '-lainen' adjectives: 'Millainen sää on?' – 'Aurinkoinen.' Spoken: 'minkälainen' or 'millanen'.
Spoken Finnish says 'mä'. Often dropped, since the verb ending already shows the person: 'Olen suomalainen'. Forms: 'minun' (my), 'minua' (me, partitive), 'minulla' (at me).
Spoken: 'sä'. Finns use the familiar 'sinä' with almost everyone; the polite plural 'te' is kept for the elderly and very formal settings. 'Sinun' = your, 'sinua' = you (partitive).
One gender-neutral pronoun for he and she; Finnish has no 'his/her' distinction either. In speech 'se' (it) is normally used for people instead.
'Meillä on' = we have. In speech the passive stands in for 'we': 'me mennään' instead of 'me menemme'.
Plural 'you', also the polite singular ('teitittely'). 'Teillä on' = you have. Spoken plural: 'te ootte' for 'te olette'.
Pronounced 'heh', nothing to do with English 'he'. Used for people; spoken Finnish prefers 'ne' (those). 'Heillä on' = they have.
Means 'it' and 'that (one)'. In speech it also replaces 'hän' for people. Forms: 'sen' (its), 'sitä' (partitive), 'siellä' (there), 'siitä' (about it).
Spoken: 'tää'. Forms: 'tämän' (of this), 'tätä' (partitive), 'tässä' (here, in this). Plural 'nämä' (these).
Spoken: 'toi'. Points at something visible; 'se' refers to something already mentioned. The partitive 'tuota...' is the Finnish 'um...' filler.
Estonian also uses 'ja'. In lists Finnish writes no comma before 'ja': 'kahvi, tee ja mehu'. 'Sekä ... että' = both ... and.
Spoken: 'mut'. After a negative, 'vaan' is used instead: 'ei tänään, vaan huomenna' (not today but tomorrow). A comma always precedes 'mutta'.
Two 'or's: 'tai' in statements ('kahvia tai teetä'), 'vai' in questions offering a choice ('Kahvia vai teetä?').
In negative sentences it becomes 'myöskään' (either): 'en minäkään' = me neither. The clitic '-kin' does the same job: 'minäkin' = me too. Spoken: 'kans'.
'Vain yksi' = just one. Spoken Finnish often says 'vaan', which in standard Finnish means 'but rather'. 'Ainoastaan' is the formal synonym.

example.en: I speak only a little Finnish.

note: 'En tule, koska olen sairas' = I'm not coming because I'm ill. In speech 'koska' also means 'when?' ('Koska tulet?'). A comma precedes it.
Introduces a clause and is always preceded by a comma: 'Luulen, että sataa' (I think that it's raining). Spoken: 'et'. Not to be confused with 'ette' (you don't).
Irregular comparison: 'parempi' (better), 'paras' (best). Partitive 'hyvää' appears in every wish: 'Hyvää päivää', 'Hyvää joulua'.
'Huono' is bad in quality or health ('huono sää', 'huono olo'); 'paha' is bad morally or in taste ('paha mieli' = hurt feelings). 'Huonompi' = worse.
The everyday word; 'suuri' is 'big, great' in a loftier register ('Suuri Pohjan sota'). 'Iso-Britannia' = Great Britain. 'Isompi' = bigger.
Genitive 'pienen', partitive 'pientä'. In compounds the prefix is 'pikku-': 'pikkuveli' = little brother, 'pikkujoulu' = pre-Christmas party.
Genitive 'uuden', partitive 'uutta'. Estonian 'uus', Hungarian 'új'. 'Uusimaa' (new land) is the region around Helsinki; 'uutiset' = the news.
Used for both people and things. 'Vanhempi' = older (and 'parent'), 'vanhin' = oldest. 'Vanhainkoti' = old people's home.
Genitive 'nuoren'. 'Nuoriso' = youth (collectively), 'nuorempi' = younger. Estonian 'noor'.
One word for long and tall: 'pitkä matka' = a long way, 'pitkä mies' = a tall man. Gradation 'pitkän'. 'Pitkään' = for a long time.
Genitive 'lyhyen'. Also for people: 'lyhyt mies'. 'Lyhyesti' = briefly, 'lyhenne' = abbreviation.
Genitive 'kauniin', partitive 'kaunista'. 'Kaunis sää' = beautiful weather, 'kauneus' = beauty.
'Ruma sana' (ugly word) = a swear word. 'Rumempi' = uglier.
'Nopeasti' = quickly, 'nopeus' = speed. Partitive 'nopeaa'. Adverbs are formed with '-sti'.
Genitive 'hitaan'. The adverb 'hitaasti' is the learner's best friend: 'Puhu hitaasti!' = Speak slowly!
Gradation 'helpon'. 'Helposti' = easily, 'helpompi' = easier. 'Helppo nakki' = a piece of cake (literally an easy sausage).
Partitive 'vaikeaa'. 'Suomi on vaikea kieli' (Finnish is a hard language) is what every Finn will tell you. 'Vaikeus' = difficulty.
Partitive 'tärkeää': 'Se on tärkeää' = it is important. 'Tärkein' = the most important.
Comfortable of things ('mukava tuoli') and pleasant of people and events: 'Oli mukava tavata' = It was nice to meet you. The written counterpart of spoken 'kiva'.
From 'kiinnostaa' (to interest). The synonym 'mielenkiintoinen' is literally 'mind-interesting'. 'Olen kiinnostunut' = I am interested.
Genitive 'puhtaan'. 'Puhdas vesi' = clean water, 'puhtaus' = cleanliness. Also 'pure': 'puhdasta villaa' = pure wool.
From 'lika' (dirt). Genitive 'likaisen'. 'Likaantua' = to get dirty.
'Vahva kahvi' = strong coffee. 'Vahvuus' = strength; 'voimakas' is strong in the sense of powerful.
Gradation 'heikon'. 'Heikko jää' (weak ice) is the spring warning on every Finnish lake. 'Heikkous' = weakness.
Genitive 'täyden', partitive 'täyttä'. 'Täysin' = completely, 'täysi-ikäinen' = of legal age. 'Olen täynnä' = I'm full (after eating).
'Tyhjä pullo' = empty bottle. 'Tyhjentää' = to empty, 'tyhjä' is also 'blank' on a form.
Gradation 'oudon'. 'Outoa' = that's odd. 'Kummallinen' and 'omituinen' are synonyms.
From Swedish 'köping' (market town). Gradation 'nk' → 'ng': 'kaupungin', 'kaupungissa' (in the city). 'Pääkaupunki' = capital.

example.en: Helsinki is the capital of Finland.

note: From 'keski' (middle). 'Keskustassa' = downtown, 'keskustaan' = to the centre. Also the name of the Centre Party.
Also 'a visit': 'olla kylässä' = to be visiting someone, 'tulla kylään' = to come over. Estonian 'küla'.
From Swedish 'kyrka'. Gradation 'kirkon', 'kirkossa' = in church. Helsinki's white 'Tuomiokirkko' (cathedral) dominates the Senate Square.
'Kirja' + the collective suffix '-sto'. Finland's public libraries are among the busiest in the world; Helsinki's 'Oodi' is the showpiece.
From Swedish 'museum' with the ending reshaped. 'Museossa' = in the museum. 'Kansallismuseo' = the National Museum.
From Swedish 'teater'. 'Kansallisteatteri' = the National Theatre. Finnish doubles the 't' to keep the stress pattern.
From 'puu' (tree) + the collective suffix '-sto'. 'Puistossa' = in the park. 'Kansallispuisto' = national park.
From Swedish 'strand' with the 'st' reduced to 't'. Gradation 'rannan', 'rannalla' = on the beach. 'Uimaranta' = swimming beach.
'Uima-' (from 'uida') + 'halli' (hall). Every town has one, with a sauna attached. 'Uima-allas' = the pool itself.
From Swedish 'post'. Means both the post office and the mail: 'Onko postia?' = Is there any mail? 'Postimerkki' = stamp.
'Poliisi' (from Swedish 'polis') + 'asema'. 'Poliisi' is also a single police officer. Emergency number: 112.
Loan with the Finnish '-i'. 'Baarissa' = at the bar. 'Pubi' and 'kapakka' (a dive) are alternatives.
'Kunto' (fitness, condition) + 'sali' (hall, from Swedish 'sal'). 'Käydä salilla' = to go to the gym. 'Hyvässä kunnossa' = in good shape.
'Elokuva' (film) is 'elo' (life) + 'kuva' (picture). In speech a film is a 'leffa' and the cinema is simply 'leffateatteri' or 'leffa'.

example.en: Shall we go to the cinema?

note: From 'rakentaa' (to build). Genitive 'rakennuksen'. 'Rakennustyömaa' = building site.
Gradation 'paikan'. 'Paikalla' = on the spot, present; 'paikallinen' = local. Also a seat: 'Onko tämä paikka vapaa?' = Is this seat free?
From 'osoittaa' (to point, to indicate). Genitive 'osoitteen'. 'Mikä sinun osoitteesi on?' = What is your address?
Capitalised for the country, lower-case 'suomi' for the language. Genitive 'Suomen', 'Suomessa' = in Finland. The origin of the name is debated; 'Finland' is the Swedish name.

example.en: I live in Finland and speak Finnish.

note: The '-lainen' suffix makes nationalities and adjectives from places: 'englantilainen', 'ruotsalainen', 'helsinkiläinen'. Not capitalised.
Country, land, soil and earth in one: 'maalla' = in the countryside, 'maapallo' = the globe, 'kotimaa' = homeland. Estonian 'maa'.
From 'auki' (open). A paved public square; the market square is 'tori'. 'Senaatintori' = Senate Square.
Appears in place names: 'Suomenlinna' (sea fortress off Helsinki), 'Savonlinna', 'Hämeenlinna'. 'Linnanmäki' is Helsinki's amusement park. Slang for prison.
Object in the partitive: 'Etsin asemaa' = I'm looking for the station. 'Etsivä' = detective.
Gradation 't' → 'd': 'löydän'. The passive-like 'löytyy' is everywhere: 'Löytyykö kahvia?' = Is there any coffee? 'Löytö' = a find.
